claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys is mainly governed by the degree of local atomic disorder.
Local atomic disorder affects the electron-phonon coupling strength involved in Cooper-pair formation.
The initial as-cast high-entropy alloy is a disordered solid solution that exhibits superconductivity.
Controlled annealing can systematically reduce atomic disorder while overall composition remains constant.
Local atomic disorder influences electron-scattering processes.
Local atomic disorder induces variations in local lattice distortions.
Reducing disorder through annealing alters phonon modes.
Reducing disorder through annealing alters electron scattering.
Disorder-induced changes in phonon modes and electron scattering diminish or otherwise modify superconducting pairing interactions.
Annealed samples with reduced disorder will have a lower superconducting critical temperature than the highly disordered as-cast baseline.
Annealed samples with reduced disorder will show altered electron-phonon coupling features relative to the as-cast baseline.
The proposed mechanism is significant only in high-entropy alloys or other systems with substantial compositional complexity and inherent atomic disorder.
Simpler alloys or alloys with minimal disorder may not show the same superconducting sensitivity to changes in disorder.
Tunneling spectroscopy can be used to determine an electron-phonon coupling constant.
X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy can assess the degree of atomic order or disorder relevant to the proposed comparison.

contradictions.description: The conditions require experiments to be conducted below the anticipated Tc, whereas determining Tc ordinarily requires measurements spanning the superconducting transition rather than remaining entirely below it.
